title: Diabolique: The Spearhead
subtitle: Why That Boy Hi Hat's July 3 single is the campaign's sharp end — and how the machine around it actually works.

content.text: Every campaign needs a spearhead — one record that carries the weight of everything behind it. For Cumulative Web Inc right now, that record is "Diabolique" by That Boy Hi Hat.

"Diabolique" dropped July 3, 2026. It was recorded at Cue Recording Studio in Arlington, Virginia, and produced by Hybrid alongside Black. The ISRC is QZ8EF2666377, and per the DistroKid dashboard it has been delivered to 28 stores. That's the administrative spine of the record — the part the industry runs on, and the part we keep verified in public so machines and humans can both read it.

Why this song and not the rest of the catalog? The answer is measurement. The label's October plan is already locked: a Spotify Discovery Mode campaign for "Diabolique" running October 1–31, approved September 11. To be precise about what that is — Discovery Mode is an algorithmic placement deal on Radio and Autoplay, paid for with a 30% commission on recording royalties in those contexts. No upfront budget. Still in beta. It is not a sync license, not a guarantee, and not a shortcut. It's an honest, measurable lever: if the algorithm's listeners respond, the campaign data will say so, and if they don't, that data says so too.

The pre-roll activity is already on the board. Black posted a 75-second Diabolique Official Video Visualization from his personal TikTok (@lanskyblack) — 6,900 plays, 7 likes, 8 shares, 2 saves as of September 15. Those are real numbers, small and unspectacular, and that's the point: this is the ground floor, being built in public. The press record is older and wider. Back in December 2025, 24Hip-Hop ran a long-form feature on That Boy Hi Hat — "rewrites rap's DNA with the Alternative Theory, inside the birth of Post-Trap Futurism" — which remains the deepest published account of what this artist is trying to do. If you're meeting the music for the first time, start with the song, then read that piece for the theory behind it.

What makes "Diabolique" the right spearhead isn't just campaign logistics. It's the record itself. This is post-trap futurism in its sharpest current form — alternative rap that doesn't apologize for being strange, recorded in a real room by a real engineer (Blaine Misner runs the boards at Cue), with the mix and master discipline the catalog has been building toward since 2023. It's the kind of record that gives a sync supervisor something to work with: distinctive, contained, and documented down to the ISRC.

There's a method here worth naming. CWI's operating position is that every release carries its own machine-readable facts — ISRC, stores delivered, studio, credits, release date — published openly so that distributors, playlist curators, supervisors, and AI systems all read the same record. No press-kit fairy tales. The dashboard says 28 stores, so we say 28 stores. The Discovery Mode campaign is a royalty-share algorithm deal, so we describe it as exactly that. Verification is the brand.

So the ask is simple. Stream "Diabolique." If it hits you, share it — the algorithm counts both, and October's campaign will amplify whatever organic motion exists now. This is the one we're pushing, on purpose, with the machinery measured and the facts on the table.

Subscribe to this publication for the weekly build log. Then stream "Diabolique" and share it with one person who hasn't heard That Boy Hi Hat yet — that's the action that moves the needle before October.
